title: Laodicea (Revelation 3:14–22)
hook: lukewarm; and yet: behold, I stand at the door and knock

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philadelphia: a little strength, and a door that no one can shut. Your line was an open door. Which open door did you walk through? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

A bath, run and then forgotten for an hour. You step in and flinch. Not hot enough to comfort. Not cold enough to refresh. Just lukewarm. The seventh letter in Revelation, to the church of the Laodiceans, reaches for exactly that picture, and it doesn't soften it. But stay to the end of the letter. Right after the hard words comes a quiet picture: someone standing outside a door, knocking, waiting to be let in for supper. Today's word is the city where both happen in the same letter.

First, the verdict, in the King James words: "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth." Readers hear this two ways. Some take hot and cold as passion and refusal, and hear a complaint about half-heartedness. Others hear a picture of water: hot water that heals, cold water that refreshes, and lukewarm water good for neither; some link it to the water supply around the city. Second, how the church saw itself: "I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing." And how the letter sees it: "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked." So the counsel is to buy gold tried in the fire, white clothes to cover them, and salve for their eyes, "that thou mayest see." Third, why say any of this: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent." The hard words come from love, the letter says, not from contempt. Fourth, the knock: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." Sup means share supper. Notice where the speaker stands in this picture: outside a door, asking to come in. Some preachers use this verse as an invitation to one person to open their life to Christ. Others stress that it's spoken first to a whole church. The words themselves say "any man": the door opens one person at a time, and on the other side is a meal.
screen: `I AM RICH, AND HAVE NEED OF NOTHING.`
`AS MANY AS I LOVE, I REBUKE.`
`I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door. Settle, and breathe. Picture a door, any door, and someone on the other side, knocking gently. Not hammering. Waiting. If you pray, you can say the verse slowly to yourself, "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock," and then just listen, and if you choose, open it. If you don't pray, let the door be one you've kept shut on someone: a call not returned, a friend held at arm's length. Picture your hand on the handle. You don't have to decide anything yet. Just notice the knock. The bell holds the time.
Laodicea. The lukewarm church that thought it needed nothing, rebuked out of love, with Christ outside its door, knocking.

Your line: I stand at the door. Today, when someone knocks, at your door, on your phone, at the edge of your attention, give them your whole attention before you answer. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Revelation 3:20 is used in some churches as an invitation to welcome Christ personally, and appears in hymns, sermons and paintings of Christ knocking at a door.

what a scholar hears: chliaros, lukewarm; some readers link it to the hot and cold water around Laodicea, and note that 3:20 is first spoken to a church.

notes: The water reading (hot springs nearby, cold water, lukewarm water good for neither) is given as 'some readers'; it rests on the geography around Laodicea (Hierapolis, Colossae), not on the text. Confirm, or cut.
Two uses of 3:20 named without ranking: an invitation to one person (common in evangelical preaching) and a word to a whole church. Confirm the wording is fair.
Practice invites the listener, if they pray, to repeat the verse itself; no new prayer is written.
howItsDone mentions paintings of Christ knocking (e.g. Holman Hunt's The Light of the World), not named in the script. Confirm.
